title: Allah, the One
hookLine: one, eternal, merciful, like nothing else

cards: How short can a description of God be? The Qur'an gives one in four short verses.
The chapter is called al-Ikhlas, sincerity, and it sits near the very end of the book, small enough to learn in a sitting and said in prayer.
Day one hundred sixty-two met the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari where the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says it equals a third of the Qur'an. Four verses, worth a third. Today they open the first article of faith.

teach.b: Here it is, in Pickthall's translation. "Say: He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten. And there is none comparable unto Him." A line at a time.
First, one. Not one among several, and not the first of a series.
Muslims call this tawhid, oneness, and it's the center of the whole list of six. Second, eternally besought. The Arabic word is as-Samad, and translators struggle with it.
Pickthall's phrase points to the one everyone turns to, who needs nothing from anyone. Every other thing leans on something; this One doesn't lean. Third, nothing like Him.
Another verse says it plainly: "Naught is as His likeness." Some readers see here one reason Islamic art leaves out pictures of God and turns to calligraphy and pattern instead.
Fourth, merciful. The surah doesn't say it, but the line said before surah after surah does: "In the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful." Oneness in Islam isn't cold.
And a word about the name. Allah is the Arabic word for God. Arabic-speaking Christians say Allah in their prayers and their Bibles, and Arabic-speaking Jews have used it as well.
The name is shared; what Muslims say about Him is in those four verses.

how: Muslims recite Surah al-Ikhlas often, in daily prayers and at other times, and the oneness of God, tawhid, stands at the center of Islamic belief.

games.q: a friend asks how the Qur'an sums up God in a few lines. what do you point to?
o: a long list of names and deeds.
four verses: one, besought of all, not begetting nor begotten, none comparable.
a picture of a king on a throne.
games.why: Surah al-Ikhlas does it in four short verses, and a hadith says they equal a third of the Qur'an.

practice: Notice how many things are in your mind right now, a message to answer, a sound outside, a worry, and let them be many.

Then rest on one thing, your breath or the single word one, and come back to it each time the many pull you away. If you pray, you can recite al-Ikhlas slowly, or simply the word Allah; if not, the word one is enough.
